name: Gravitational Waves in Friedmann Universes
description: Exact gravitational waves with distinct fronts running into Friedmann universes filled with a stiff fluid, $p = \rho$, found by Jiří Bičák and Jerry B. Griffiths in 1994 and 1996. The fronts are planes or cylinders in the open and flat universes and tori in the closed one, and each wave is partly reflected, so the field behind its front is algebraically general.
convention: We use signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and $G=c=1$, with $R_{\mu\nu}=R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$; every chart is Bičák and Griffiths's line element multiplied by $-1$ [bicak1996]. The coordinates are dimensionless, $\gamma$ is an area, the fluid is at rest in every chart, and $R$ and $K$ are the Ricci and Kretschmann scalars.
history: Sound in a stiff fluid, whose pressure equals its energy density, $p = \rho$, travels at the speed of light, along the same characteristics as a gravitational wave [bicak1994]. Jiří Bičák of Charles University in Prague and Jerry B. Griffiths of the University of Technology in Loughborough sent a gravitational wave into an open Friedmann universe filled with this fluid, and published the solution in January 1994 [bicak1994]. Ahead of the wave front the universe is homogeneous and isotropic, and its Weyl tensor is zero [bicak1994]. Behind the front the field is algebraically general, since the wave is partly reflected as it travels [bicak1994]. Bičák and Griffiths wrote that most exact work on gravitational radiation "has been concentrated on space-times which are either flat asymptotically or contain flat regions explicitly" [bicak1994].¶They noted that earlier exact waves in cosmology extended over whole universes, with no wave surface whose geometry could be analysed [bicak1996]. Romualdo Tabensky and Abraham Haskel Taub discussed a shock wave in a plane symmetric stiff fluid in 1973 [tabensky1973]. Joan Centrella and Richard Matzner collided plane gravitational waves in expanding vacuum universes in 1982 and found the singularity in the past, at the big bang [centrella1982]. Griffiths had sent a wave of constant linear polarisation into the spatially flat stiff universe in 1993 and found it partly reflected [griffiths1993stiff, bicak1994]. Bičák and Griffiths left the potential of the fluid unchanged across the wave front, which excludes sound waves of the type Tabensky and Taub considered [bicak1996].¶A plane wave needs flat fronts, and Bičák and Griffiths found them in the open universe, whose space at each moment is a hyperboloid in a flat spacetime of four dimensions [bicak1994]. Null hyperplanes of that spacetime cut the hyperboloid in surfaces whose intrinsic geometry is flat and which extend to infinity in two directions [bicak1994, bicak1996]. The 3-sphere of the closed universe has no such sections [bicak1994]. Bičák and Griffiths wrote the three stiff Friedmann universes out in conformal time $\eta$, since they had not found them given explicitly [bicak1994]. The scale factor $a$ obeys $a^2 = \gamma\sinh 2\eta$, $2\gamma\eta$, or $\gamma\sin 2\eta$ in the open, flat, and closed cases, with $\gamma$ a constant with the dimensions of an area [bicak1994]. The function $V$ that stretches one direction along the front and shrinks the other obeys a linear equation, so waves add to one another and to the background [bicak1996].¶In the Weyl tensor behind the front, $\Psi_4$ is the wave that advances, $\Psi_0$ the part scattered back, and $\Psi_2$ the interaction of the two [bicak1996]. Bičák and Griffiths also collided two such waves head on in the open universe [bicak1994]. After the collision the spacetime "continues to expand indefinitely", and the future spacelike singularities of plane waves colliding in flat space "apparently do not occur" [bicak1994]. They found this consistent with a theorem on colliding plane waves that Frank Tipler gave in 1980, since the singularity of these universes lies in the past [bicak1994, tipler1980]. Alexander Feinstein and Griffiths reported a future spacelike curvature singularity for colliding waves in a closed universe later in 1994 [feinstein1994]. Griffiths and Georgii A. Alekseev of the Steklov Mathematical Institute in Moscow gave complete solutions in 1995 for such waves in the flat and open stiff universes and in a vacuum Kasner universe [alekseev1995].¶Apart from their wave fronts these solutions are regular everywhere after the big bang, and even arbitrarily strong waves of the family "are not sufficient to halt and reverse the expansion" [alekseev1995]. Bičák and Griffiths worked out the wave fronts of all three universes in 1996, planes or cylinders in the flat and the open ones and tori in the closed one [bicak1996]. A plane front may contain an impulse, a step, or a Weyl tensor with any finite number of continuous derivatives, and the plane waves are singular only at the big bang [bicak1996]. Cylindrical and toroidal fronts may contain steps and no impulses, and their waves have a further curvature singularity on the axis they leave, which Bičák and Griffiths considered both "source" and "absorber" of the waves [bicak1996]. A torus divides the 3-sphere of the closed universe into two solid tori, and a shock wave that leaves the axis of one at the big bang converges on the axis of the other at the big crunch [bicak1996]. Bičák and Griffiths identified the waves of Feinstein and Griffiths as these toroidal ones, singular at the big bang, at the big crunch, and on the axis, in closed universes of Gowdy type [bicak1996].¶Alekseev and Griffiths built vacuum counterparts in 1996, waves with cylindrical, spherical, and toroidal fronts that run into flat space from singular sources [alekseev1996wavefronts]. They related the waves with distinct fronts in 1997, those in Friedmann universes included, to a generalisation of the cylindrical pulse of Nathan Rosen [alekseev1997]. All of them had one fixed linear polarisation, and Alekseev and Griffiths added a cylindrical pulse in flat space with two states of polarisation [alekseev1997]. Bičák wrote in a review of 2000 that colliding plane waves had been studied mostly for "non-classical" issues since 1991, and named these collisions in expanding universes among the few exceptions [bicak2000exact]. Bičák and Griffiths had written that waves in dust, or in fluids with a more realistic equation of state, raise "difficult and important problems" [bicak1996]. José M. M. Senovilla and Raül Vera found in 2001 a gravitational wave in an anisotropic universe of Bianchi type V with $p = \rho/3$, which "seems to be the first explicit exact example" of its kind [senovilla2001].

related.text: Ahead of every wave front the spacetime is a Friedmann universe filled with a stiff fluid, open, flat or closed [bicak1996]. Its Weyl tensor vanishes, so the Weyl tensor behind the front belongs to the waves alone [bicak1994].

The same matter with two commuting Killing vectors. Alekseev and Griffiths generated their stiff fluid waves by the method of John Wainwright, W. C. W. Ince and B. J. Marshman [alekseev1995, wainwright1979stiff].

A closed Friedmann universe with toroidal waves is a Gowdy-type spacetime filled with a stiff fluid. Its two commuting, hypersurface orthogonal Killing vectors have tori for orbits, and the wave fronts are those tori [bicak1996].

Plane gravitational waves colliding in flat space, where the collision ends in a future spacelike singularity. In the expanding open universe of stiff fluid such singularities "apparently do not occur" [bicak1994].

Cylindrical gravitational waves in vacuum. Nathan Rosen built a pulse of them with a distinct front, and Alekseev and Griffiths related the waves in Friedmann universes to a generalisation of that pulse [alekseev1997].
Plane waves with distinct fronts also run into a vacuum Kasner universe, for which Alekseev and Griffiths gave complete solutions [alekseev1995].

coordinates.name: Plane Wave, Flat Universe

parameters.description: Positive area that sets the scale of the universe.
Dimensionless amplitude of the wave, any real number; $A=0$ is the flat universe.
Profile $H_2(z/\eta)$ of Alekseev and Griffiths, zero on the front $z=\eta$ and $1$ at $z=-\eta$.
The wave, which stretches $x$ and shrinks $y$ along the front.
Change the wave makes in the conformal factor, zero on the front and negative behind it.

coordinates.convention: Bičák and Griffiths's (1.1) and (7.1)-(7.3) with $e^{-U}=2\eta$ and $e^{-M}=2\eta e^{-S}$ [bicak1996], and the one term profile of Alekseev and Griffiths with $n=2$ [alekseev1995]; the front $z=\eta$ moves toward $+z$, ahead of it is the flat planar chart, and $\rho=p=3e^{S}/(64\pi\gamma\eta^3)$.
geodesics: \ddot{\eta} + \dfrac{2 + A^2\,K^2\,\eta^4 + 4A^2\,H^2\,\eta^4 + A^2\,K^2\,\eta^2\,z^2 - 4A^2\,H\,K\,\eta^3\,z}{4\eta}\dot{\eta}^2 + A^2\,K\,\eta^2\left(2H\,\eta - K\,z\right)\dot{\eta}\dot{z} + \dfrac{2 + A^2\,K^2\,\eta^4 + 4A^2\,H^2\,\eta^4 + A^2\,K^2\,\eta^2\,z^2 - 4A^2\,H\,K\,\eta^3\,z}{4\eta}\dot{z}^2 + \dfrac{\left(2A\,H\,\eta^2 - A\,K\,\eta\,z + 1\right)e^{S}e^{V}}{2\eta}\dot{x}^2 + \dfrac{\left(1 + A\,K\,\eta\,z - 2A\,H\,\eta^2\right)e^{-V}e^{S}}{2\eta}\dot{y}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Flat Universe, Planar

parameters.description: Positive area that sets the scale of the universe.

coordinates.convention: Bičák and Griffiths's (2.4) with $a^2=2\gamma\eta$ [bicak1996]; $x$ and $y$ span the planes of constant $\eta$ and $z$, and $\rho=p=3/(64\pi\gamma\eta^3)$.

coordinates.name: Flat Universe, Cylindrical

parameters.description: Positive area that sets the scale of the universe.

coordinates.convention: Bičák and Griffiths's (2.5) with $a^2=2\gamma\eta$ [bicak1996], $r$ for their radius; the null surfaces of constant $\eta-r$ are cylinders about $r=0$.

coordinates.name: Open Universe, Planar

parameters.description: Positive area that sets the scale of the universe.

coordinates.convention: Bičák and Griffiths's (3.15) with $a^2=\gamma\sinh2\eta$ [bicak1996], from the hyperboloid coordinates of their (2.6)-(2.13) [bicak1994]; the surfaces of constant $\eta$ and $\mu$ are flat planes, and $\rho=p=3/(8\pi\gamma\sinh^32\eta)$.

coordinates.name: Open Universe, Cylindrical

parameters.description: Positive area that sets the scale of the universe.

coordinates.convention: Bičák and Griffiths's (3.16) with $a^2=\gamma\sinh2\eta$ [bicak1996], $r$ for their radius, written with $\tfrac12\sinh2r\tanh r=\sinh^2r$ and $\tfrac12\sinh2r\coth r=\cosh^2r$.

coordinates.name: Closed Universe, Toroidal

parameters.description: Positive area that sets the scale of the universe.

coordinates.convention: Bičák and Griffiths's (4.7) with $a^2=\gamma\sin2\eta$ [bicak1996]; the surfaces of constant $\eta$ and $\zeta$ are tori, $\zeta=0$ and $\zeta=\pi/2$ are the circles at their two axes, and $\rho=p=3/(8\pi\gamma\sin^32\eta)$.
